caseName: Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v. Cherryland Mall Ltd. Partnership
keyFacts: Cherryland Mall Limited Partnership borrowed $8.7M in a CMBS loan secured by a Traverse City, Michigan shopping mall. Guarantor David Schostak signed a standard non-recourse carve-out ("bad boy") guaranty. The borrower became insolvent, which the loan documents' single-purpose-entity covenants separately prohibited. The lender argued insolvency alone triggered full-recourse liability under the carve-out, even absent fraud or waste.
outcome: Trial court and Court of Appeals held the guarantor personally liable for the full loan deficiency after the mall's foreclosure sale, because the borrower's insolvency breached the SPE covenant and triggered the springing full-recourse carve-out. (While on appeal, the Michigan legislature passed the Non-Recourse Mortgage Loan Act specifically to reverse this outcome prospectively, but it did not undo the judgment against Schostak.)
dollarAmountBasis: Deficiency between the $8.7M loan balance and the mall's foreclosure-sale value, for which the guarantor was held personally liable (reported as just over $2.1M).
notes: One of the most-cited post-financial-crisis 'bad boy' guaranty cases; became the catalyst for Michigan's Non-Recourse Mortgage Loan Act. Widely covered by McDermott, Law360, and CommercialSearch.

caseName: CSFB 2001-CP-4 Princeton Park Corporate Center, LLC v. SB Rental I, LLC
court: New Jersey Superior Court, Appellate Division
keyFacts: SB Rental I, LLC borrowed $13.3M secured by a first mortgage on commercial property in South Brunswick, NJ, with a non-recourse note carved out by a guaranty of payment from SB Rental's principals. SB Rental obtained $400,000 in subordinate financing in May 2004 without the lender's written consent (in violation of the note's carve-out trigger), repaid that subordinate debt seven months later, then defaulted on the primary mortgage in May 2006.
outcome: Trial court granted summary judgment holding the borrower and guarantors personally liable for the full loan amount. Appellate Division affirmed, holding as a matter of first impression in New Jersey that a non-recourse carve-out triggered by unauthorized subordinate financing fixes liability (not merely an estimate of damages) and is fully enforceable even though the triggering breach (the $400K loan) had long since been cured.
dollarAmountBasis: Personal judgment entered against the borrower and guarantors, per the Appellate Division opinion ($5,195,932.72).
notes: Frequently cited alongside Cherryland as one of the two leading 2009-2011 appellate decisions establishing that minor, cured covenant breaches can still spring full personal recourse under a bad-boy guaranty.

caseName: 51382 Gratiot Avenue Holdings, LLC v. Chesterfield Development Co., LLC
court: U.S. District Court, Eastern District of Michigan
keyFacts: Chesterfield Development borrowed $17M secured by the Chesterfield Village Square shopping center at Gratiot Avenue and 23 Mile Road, Chesterfield Township, Michigan. The loan documents included a single-purpose-entity covenant barring the borrower from becoming insolvent or failing to pay debts as they came due; guarantor John Damico's guaranty made him liable in full if that covenant was breached. The borrower defaulted on December 1, 2009 and the lender foreclosed, selling the property for $7.6M against the outstanding note.
outcome: Following the Cherryland precedent, the district court granted the lender summary judgment, holding that the borrower's insolvency breached the SPE covenant and triggered full-recourse liability against the guarantor for the entire deficiency.
dollarAmountBasis: Deficiency the lender sought and was awarded between the $17M note balance and the $7.6M foreclosure-sale value of the property ($12,240,108.64).
notes: A companion case to Cherryland on nearly identical facts (same SPE-insolvency-covenant theory), illustrating how quickly the theory spread across Michigan CMBS-backed retail loans in 2011-2012.

caseName: K.M.C. Co., Inc. v. Irving Trust Co.
court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
keyFacts: K.M.C., a wholesale/retail grocery business, held a $3.5M revolving line of credit from Irving Trust secured by accounts receivable and inventory. Without prior notice, Irving refused to advance an $800,000 draw that would have brought the balance close to the credit limit, even though the loan agreement gave Irving discretion over individual advances. K.M.C. collapsed shortly after.
outcome: Jury found Irving Trust breached an implied duty of good faith by cutting off funding without notice, and awarded $7.5M in damages plus pre-judgment interest; the Sixth Circuit affirmed, holding the lender owed a duty to give notice before exercising discretion to stop funding.
dollarAmountBasis: Jury verdict for breach of the implied covenant of good faith (wrongful cutoff of funding), affirmed on appeal, plus pre-judgment interest not separately quantified here.
notes: The underlying collateral was a working-capital line secured by receivables/inventory, not real property — this is not a CRE-secured loan. It is included because it is the foundational lender-liability precedent (implied covenant of good faith, notice-before-cutoff duty) that is routinely cited in commercial real estate lender-liability litigation, including in more recent CRE cases like the Steinway Tower dispute below.

court: California Court of Appeal, Fourth Appellate District
keyFacts: Bank of America financed a real estate construction loan and, according to the borrower/developer's suit, exerted improper day-to-day control over the construction project beyond a normal lender's oversight role, deviating from accepted banking practice.
outcome: After a three-month trial, the jury found the bank liable for improperly controlling the construction project and awarded $6.6M in punitive damages (with compensatory damages determined separately); the Court of Appeal later reversed on an unrelated jury-instruction issue regarding constructive fraud and remanded.
dollarAmountBasis: Punitive damages verdict against the bank for improper control/lender-liability conduct on a real estate construction loan; the separately-tried compensatory damages figure was not confirmed in the sources reviewed for this entry.
notes: One of the classic 1980s 'lender control' liability cases taught alongside K.M.C. and State National Bank of El Paso v. Farah Manufacturing. The reported punitive verdict is confirmed by multiple secondary sources; the compensatory damages amount and final post-remand disposition were not independently verified.

caseName: The Ardent Companies (Ardent Cos.) v. Baruch Broad Street LLC / Zamir Equities
citation: Franklin County Court of Common Pleas, Ohio (case no. not independently verified)
court: Franklin County Court of Common Pleas
keyFacts: Atlanta-based Ardent Companies loaned $11.8M in January 2022 to Baruch Broad Street LLC (controlled by New York-based Asher Roshanzamir/Zamir Equities) to buy the 21-story former KeyBank tower at 88 E. Broad St. in downtown Columbus. The borrower defaulted; the building fell into disrepair (bounced vendor checks, a stuck elevator, threatened water shutoff). Ardent filed a foreclosure complaint and receivership motion in April 2024; a receiver was appointed May 2024.
outcome: Ardent's complaint sought a money judgment of $9,320,807 against the borrower/guarantor in addition to foreclosure. After more than a year under receivership, the property was sold at a April 2026 foreclosure auction for $5.1M — less than half its 2022 purchase price of roughly $12M and well short of the ~$9.3M owed, leaving a substantial unrecovered deficiency.
dollarAmountBasis: Amount Ardent sought in its foreclosure complaint's money judgment against the borrower ($9,320,807), representing principal, interest, and fees outstanding on the original $11.8M loan; the property later sold at auction for only $5.1M.
notes: Illustrates the gap between a defaulted loan balance and eventual auction recovery on a distressed downtown office tower — a $11.8M loan produced a $9.3M claimed debt but only a $5.1M sale, i.e., roughly a 45% recovery against the claimed debt. Reported by NBC4 Columbus, AOL/Yahoo, and Columbus Underground.

caseName: AFF IV 200 Miami LLC v. SRCTD 44-200 LLC and FS Equity Investments II LLC
citation: Miami-Dade County Circuit Court (Fla.), stipulated foreclosure judgment entered June 11, 2026
court: Eleventh Judicial Circuit Court, Miami-Dade County, Florida
keyFacts: Atlanta-based Ardent Companies provided Boca Raton-based Stonerock Capital (led by Yaakov 'Jacob' Handelsman) and partner Triple Double Real Estate a $58.3M mortgage to buy two downtown Miami office buildings — the 172,292-sq-ft Courthouse Tower at 44 W. Flagler St. and the 150,530-sq-ft building at 200 S.E. First St. — for $56.7M in 2022. The borrower defaulted, missing payments and failing to repay at the loan's June 1, 2024 maturity, with $41.1M in principal outstanding.
outcome: Miami-Dade Circuit Judge Joseph Perkins granted a stipulated final foreclosure judgment in favor of the lender (through affiliate AFF IV 200 Miami LLC) for $65.7M — $41.1M principal plus accrued interest and fees — clearing the way for both buildings to be sold at online auction.
dollarAmountBasis: Stipulated final foreclosure judgment amount entered by the court ($65.7M), comprising $41.1M in unpaid principal plus interest and fees.
notes: A clean example of a stipulated (i.e., uncontested/agreed) foreclosure judgment — the borrower did not fight the judgment amount, only the timing of the resulting auction. Reported by The Real Deal, Bisnow, and Hoodline.

caseName: Emerald Creek Capital 3 LLC v. BH3-affiliated ownership entities (Hillsboro Beach Resort)
citation: Broward County Circuit Court (Fla.), final foreclosure judgment entered April 2026
court: Seventeenth Judicial Circuit Court, Broward County, Florida
keyFacts: BH3 Management principals Daniel Lebensohn and Gregory Freedman, through ownership entities, borrowed $26M from an Emerald Creek Capital affiliate secured by an 81-room oceanfront resort at 1159 Hillsboro Mile (formerly operated by collapsed short-term-rental startup Sonder). The borrower defaulted in March 2024 by failing to pay property taxes, prompting the lender to advance roughly $731,000 and later another $2.2M to cover the tax bills; the loan then matured in August 2024 without repayment.
outcome: Broward County Circuit Judge Martin Bidwill entered a $40M final foreclosure judgment in April 2026. Emerald Creek Capital itself acquired the resort at the resulting July 16, 2026 foreclosure sale.
dollarAmountBasis: Final foreclosure judgment entered by the court ($40M), reflecting the original $26M loan plus accrued interest, fees, and the roughly $2.9M in tax advances the lender made to protect its collateral.
notes: Shows how lender-advanced protective payments (here, unpaid property taxes) compound a relatively modest original loan balance into a much larger final judgment. Reported by The Real Deal, Commercial Observer, Bisnow, and Commercial Real Estate Direct.

caseName: LNR Partners (special servicer) v. Cohen Brothers Realty Corp. (750 Lexington Avenue)
citation: Supreme Court of the State of New York, New York County (foreclosure judgment ~$155.9M, entered 2025)
court: Supreme Court of the State of New York, New York County
keyFacts: Charles Cohen personally sponsored and guaranteed a $130M refinancing of 750 Lexington Avenue (Cohen Brothers' Manhattan headquarters) in 2015, part of a CMBS pool (CGCMT 2015-GC35/GSMS 2015-GC34) that grew to a $155.9M claimed balance. Special servicer LNR Partners alleged multiple defaults, including failure to pay taxes, provide financial statements, and certify Cohen's net worth/liquidity as required by the loan. LNR filed suit in May 2024 and won summary judgment in mid-2025.
outcome: The property's appraised value had collapsed to roughly $41M (down 86% from a pre-pandemic value of about $300M). At the January 21, 2026 foreclosure auction, with an upset price of $161,854,848.66, no bidder appeared — the property reverted to lender U.S. Bank for a nominal $1,000, leaving the loan's full ~$155.9M-plus balance effectively unrecovered from the collateral.
dollarAmountBasis: Foreclosure judgment amount reported at auction ($155.9M, i.e., the CMBS loan balance including accrued interest/fees); the property itself ultimately transferred to the lender for a nominal $1,000 after the auction drew no bidders.
notes: One of the starkest illustrations in this dataset of a foreclosure judgment far exceeding recoverable collateral value — a $155.9M judgment against a building appraised at roughly $41M, which then failed to draw even a single auction bid. Reported by Crain's New York Business, The Real Deal, Commercial Real Estate Direct, and Pincus Co.

caseName: Beneficial Funding Corp. / Fred Karlton v. JB Green
citation: Miami-Dade County Circuit Court (Fla.), judgment entered October 24, 2024
court: Eleventh Judicial Circuit Court, Miami-Dade County, Florida
keyFacts: Private lenders Fred Karlton and Beneficial Funding Corp. sued JB Green (an entity managed by Jacques Berrebi and William Holly) over a defaulted loan secured by a 12-story office tower at 3150 S.W. 38th Avenue near Coconut Grove, Miami, capping a four-year legal battle.
outcome: Following a non-jury trial, Miami-Dade Circuit Judge Thomas Rebull ruled for the lenders, entering an $8.7M foreclosure judgment against the building's owner.
dollarAmountBasis: Foreclosure judgment entered after a non-jury trial ($8.7M).
notes: A smaller, privately-financed (non-CMBS) foreclosure judgment that took four years of litigation to reach trial and final judgment, illustrating that non-institutional CRE loans can take substantially longer to resolve than special-servicer-driven CMBS foreclosures.

caseName: U.S. Bank National Association v. Brookfield Republic Plaza LLC
citation: Denver District Court, Colorado, filed August 10, 2026
keyFacts: U.S. Bank, on behalf of the CMBS trust holding the loan, sued to appoint a receiver over Republic Plaza, Denver's 56-story tallest office tower, co-owned by Brookfield Properties and MetLife Investment Management, after a second maturity default on the loan (first default resolved by a July 2023 modification extending maturity to March 15, 2026, which was then also missed). Trepp lists the total CMBS debt at $230.1M; the complaint cites an approximately $130M defaulted obligation.
outcome: Complaint filed seeking appointment of a receiver rather than proceeding directly to foreclosure; as of this research, no ruling on the receivership motion had been reported.
dollarAmountBasis: No dollar judgment has been entered; the $130M figure cited is the defaulted loan obligation named in the receivership complaint, not an adjudicated dollar outcome.
notes: Sourced from CREdocket's own tracked matter (live-023). Notable for showing that even institutional ownership (Brookfield + MetLife) with one prior workout did not prevent a second maturity default within three years.

caseName: Citibank, N.A. / LNR Partners v. Golub & Company and BlueFive Capital (625 North Michigan Avenue)
citation: Cook County Circuit Court, Illinois, receiver appointed June 16, 2026
court: Circuit Court of Cook County, Illinois
keyFacts: Golub & Company and BlueFive Capital defaulted on a $50.6M CMBS loan (originated by Cantor Commercial Real Estate in 2019 at 4.63% interest) secured by the office floors of a 28-story tower on Chicago's Magnificent Mile, after occupancy fell from 91.8% (2019) to 63.8% (2025) and the debt service coverage ratio dropped to 0.96.
outcome: Cook County court granted the lender's request and appointed Scott Shefman of Friedman Real Estate Management as receiver on June 16, 2026, giving the special servicer (LNR Partners) operational control of the office component pending resolution.
dollarAmountBasis: Receivership grant carries no separate dollar judgment; the $50.6M figure is the defaulted loan balance, not an adjudicated amount.
notes: A clean, granted receivership case driven by anchor-tenant-style occupancy decline on a trophy Magnificent Mile address; the ground-floor retail condominium at the same address was foreclosed separately in 2024.

caseName: Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. (as trustee) v. Hertz Investment Group (Riverfront Plaza)
citation: Richmond Circuit Court, Virginia, receiver appointed August 27, 2025
court: Circuit Court of the City of Richmond, Virginia
keyFacts: California-based Hertz Investment Group defaulted on a $146M loan secured by the twin-tower, 950,000-sq-ft Riverfront Plaza office complex in downtown Richmond, with additional defaults expected once anchor tenant Truist Bank's lease expired. Noteholders, represented by Wells Fargo, sued in August 2025 seeking a judgment reported at more than $131M and appointment of a receiver.
outcome: The court granted the receivership motion on August 27, 2025, installing Lewis Taulbee of JLL as receiver. As of March 2026, the property remained under receivership, with the receiver managing operations and positioning the asset for sale; no foreclosure auction had yet been scheduled.
dollarAmountBasis: No final dollar judgment confirmed; the $131M and $146M figures are the amount sought in the complaint and the original loan balance, respectively, not an entered judgment.
notes: Illustrates the now-common two-step CMBS enforcement pattern: receivership first (fast, operational control), foreclosure/sale later (slower). Reported by Richmond BizSense and Virginia Business; the property had sold for $147.5M in an earlier (pre-distress) transaction.

caseName: CWCapital (special servicer) v. Kawa Capital (One Parkway North Boulevard, Deerfield)
citation: Lake County Circuit Court, Illinois, receiver granted February 11, 2026
court: Circuit Court of Lake County, Illinois
keyFacts: Special servicer CWCapital sued suburban Chicago landlord Kawa Capital over a $25M CMBS loan secured by the One Parkway North Boulevard office property in Deerfield, Illinois, seeking emergency appointment of a receiver amid mounting office-loan distress in the Chicago suburbs.
outcome: Lake County Judge Daniel Jasica granted CWCapital's emergency motion on February 11, 2026, appointing Matthew Tarshis of Frontline Real Estate Partners as receiver over the property while the underlying foreclosure litigation proceeds.
dollarAmountBasis: Receivership order carries no separate dollar judgment; $25M is the defaulted loan balance.
notes: One of several suburban Chicago office receiverships (alongside 625 N. Michigan Ave. and 181 W. Madison St.) reported in the same reporting cycle, illustrating clustered regional office distress.

caseName: Independent Bank v. Leestma Management / Adelaide Pointe
citation: Kent County Circuit Court, Michigan; receivership denied October 2025, granted January 9, 2026
keyFacts: Independent Bank sued the developer of the Adelaide Pointe marina/mixed-use project in Muskegon, Michigan, claiming default on part of a $28M loan, and sought emergency appointment of a receiver under a contractual, pre-default 'as of right' receivership clause in the loan documents.
outcome: In October 2025, Judge Curt Benson denied the bank's receivership request as premature, holding that a contractual receivership clause does not override the court's equitable discretion, and that genuine factual disputes existed over collateral value, project viability, and whether an uncured default existed. The bank renewed its motion, and on January 9, 2026, Judge Benson reversed course and appointed John Polderman of Stevenson & Bullock PLC as receiver over the Independent Bank-mortgaged properties.
dollarAmountBasis: No dollar judgment; case concerns receivership appointment only. The developer has separately discussed countersuing the lender for $35M.
notes: The single clearest example in this dataset of a court initially denying receivership (holding that contractual 'as of right' clauses don't eliminate judicial discretion) and later granting it once the factual record developed further — useful for calibrating how contested receivership requests typically resolve over a several-month window.

caseName: Wilmington Trust, N.A. v. McKnight Realty Partners affiliate (Grant Building, Pittsburgh)
citation: Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas, Pennsylvania, foreclosure filed February 2024
court: Court of Common Pleas of Allegheny County, Pennsylvania
keyFacts: Wilmington Trust filed a foreclosure action against an affiliate of McKnight Realty Partners over a $37.8M debt balance on a $38M mortgage originated in 2017, secured by the 37-story, ~460,000-sq-ft Grant Building in downtown Pittsburgh (built 1928), after Huntington Bank announced plans to vacate as the building's anchor tenant.
outcome: The property was placed into receivership, with CBRE overseeing management and marketing since early 2024/2025. As of late 2025, Connecticut-based Commonwealth Development Partners had emerged as a prospective buyer, applying for a $7M state grant toward acquisition and renovation, with a transfer of ownership anticipated by year-end 2025 — but as of this research no final foreclosure judgment or sale price had been publicly confirmed.
dollarAmountBasis: No final foreclosure judgment or completed sale price confirmed in sources reviewed; $37.8M is the claimed debt balance underlying the foreclosure complaint.
notes: A multi-year-running receivership (over two years and counting as of this research) with a prospective sale still pending — illustrates how long historic/architecturally significant downtown office receiverships can take to resolve toward an actual disposition.

caseName: 111 West 57th Investment LLC v. 111 W57 Mezz Investor LLC (Steinway Tower)
citation: New York Court of Appeals, 2026 NY Slip Op 03376, decided May 28, 2026
keyFacts: AmBase-affiliated investment vehicle 111 West 57th Investment LLC invested roughly $70M in the Steinway Tower supertall condominium project. Apollo-affiliated mezzanine lenders sold a $25M junior mezzanine loan secured by the plaintiff's equity to Spruce Capital Partners at par in 2017, despite internal models reportedly showing roughly $600M in underlying equity value; Spruce initiated a UCC Article 9 strict foreclosure two days later, wiping out the plaintiff's equity position.
outcome: New York's highest court held that the lender's contractual 'sole discretion' to assign the loan does not categorically exculpate it from implied-covenant-of-good-faith claims where the discretion is alleged to have been exercised as part of a scheme to strip a joint-venture partner's equity, reinstating the good-faith claim and remitting the case to the Supreme Court, New York County for further proceedings (while affirming dismissal of a related tortious-interference claim).
dollarAmountBasis: No damages have been awarded; the Court of Appeals ruling only reinstates the claim and remands for further proceedings. The $600M figure is the plaintiff's alleged underlying equity value at the time of the loan sale, not an adjudicated amount.
notes: Sourced from CREdocket's own tracked matter (live-010). A significant doctrinal win for borrowers on the pleading standard for lender-liability claims tied to mezzanine loan assignments and UCC strict foreclosures, but the case remains unresolved on the merits and has no disclosed dollar outcome yet.

caseName: Via Mizner Owner III LLC v. Via Mizner Lender 1 LLC (Mandarin Oriental Residences, Boca Raton)
citation: Supreme Court of the State of New York, New York County, Commercial Division, filed August 17, 2026
court: Supreme Court of the State of New York, New York County, Commercial Division
keyFacts: Penn-Florida Companies affiliates sued their construction lenders (tied to Madison Realty Capital and Apollo/Athene-affiliated entities), alleging the lenders manufactured the very defaults — including funding decisions and involvement in terminating the project's hotel management agreement — that the same lender group is now citing to justify a $417.7M judicial foreclosure (filed in Florida in July 2026) and a separate UCC Article 9 sale of the pledged project-entity equity.
outcome: Justice Andrew Borrok signed a temporary restraining order blocking the UCC Article 9 equity sale and set a hearing on preliminary relief for October 1, 2026. The case remains pending with no ruling on the merits of the $500M+ lender-liability claim.
dollarAmountBasis: No judgment or settlement; $500M+ is the amount sought in the complaint's prayer for relief, not an adjudicated or agreed figure.
notes: Sourced from CREdocket's own tracked matter (live-029), a direct counter-suit to the lender's own foreclosure action on the same project (also tracked as live-007). Useful as a live illustration of a lender-liability theory being used specifically to pause a UCC Article 9 equity-pledge foreclosure rather than the underlying mortgage foreclosure itself.

caseName: Bank Midwest, N.A. v. The Integritty Group
citation: U.S. District Court, Eastern District of Pennsylvania, filed August 6, 2026
court: U.S. District Court, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
keyFacts: Bank Midwest sued The Integritty Group ('TIG'), operator of 41 Qdoba Mexican Eats restaurants, alleging TIG defaulted on a $20M loan executed in April 2025 secured by the restaurant portfolio, concealed a 'serious liquidity problem' from the bank, and negotiated to terminate its Qdoba franchise agreement and sell the restaurants without notifying the lender — jeopardizing the collateral's going-concern value.
outcome: Complaint filed seeking roughly $18.25M in principal, interest, and fees, plus appointment of a receiver over TIG's restaurant operations; no ruling had been reported as of this research.
dollarAmountBasis: No judgment entered; $18.25M is the amount sought in the complaint against the $20M original loan.
notes: Sourced from CREdocket's own tracked matter (live-025). Included for its franchise-collateral theory (a franchisee's covert exit from its brand agreement treated as a collateral-impairment/covenant-breach event independent of payment default) even though no dollar outcome has been disclosed yet.
